VERDICT: EXTEND C0001 | `scan_health()` does not just misreport missing tools as available; it also omits unavailable tools entirely from `HealthScan.tools_available`. Evidence: when `source_paths` is empty it returns `HealthScan(elapsed_s=...)` with default `{}`, and in the normal path it only inserts keys for tools it iterates and whose runner returns/raises. Downstream, consumers cannot distinguish “tool unavailable” from “field absent”, so health reports are schema-unstable and availability checks can silently default wrong. Existing fix should ensure all expected tool keys are always populated with explicit booleans.

FINDING_ID: F001
SEVERITY: 0.95
FLAW_CLASS: 2
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.63
DESCRIPTION: FIND — `evaluate_fix()` does not sandbox imports/tests against the patched source tree; it writes only the single patched file into a temp dir and then runs the supplied `test_cmd` there unchanged. Evidence: in `evaluate_fix()`, `patched_path = os.path.join(tmpdir, os.path.basename(target_path))` writes one file only; no package tree or sibling modules are copied. Then `_run_tool(test_cmd, cwd=tmpdir)` executes the caller-provided command as-is. In the actual integration, `immune_agents.run_immune_pipeline()` calls `evaluate_fixes(..., test_cmd=["python3", "-m", "pytest", "bench/tests/", ...])`. From `cwd=tmpdir`, `bench/tests/` is typically absent, and Python imports during tests resolve against the real repo on `sys.path`, not the patched temp file. Result: the “sandbox-test proposed fixes” feature can report SAFE/NEUTRAL/HARMFUL without executing the patched code under test at all.
FOLLOW: This crosses the endocrine↔immune interface directly because Stage 4 in `immune_agents.py` sets `finding.verified = True` when endocrine returns SAFE or NEUTRAL. If tests run against the real source tree or fail to locate the test tree, reviewers get misleading verification status: broken fixes may be marked verified, and valid fixes may be judged without meaningful test coverage. It also violates the module’s stated non-modification sandbox contract by giving a false sense of isolation while still depending on live repo imports. The downstream consequence is the bug-closed gate in later rounds can suppress further reports based on a fix that was never actually exercised in sandbox.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — when evaluating a fix, copy the full relevant source tree into the temp directory preserving relative paths, apply the patch to the copied target file there, and run tests/tooling against that copied tree. The simplest sufficient implementation is: compute the repository-relative path of `target_path`, copy each `source_path` into matching relative locations under `tmpdir`, patch the copied target, and rewrite/execute `test_cmd` from the temp root so imports resolve to the sandboxed files.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F002
SEVERITY: 0.88
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.58
DESCRIPTION: FIND — `_compute_fix_verdict()` can classify a fix as `SAFE` even when it introduces new errors in one tool, as long as a different tool’s issue count decreases by a larger amount. Evidence: it computes `total_net = net_type_errors + net_ruff_errors + net_bandit_issues`; if `total_net < 0`, verdict is `SAFE`. Example from current logic: `net_type_errors=+3`, `net_ruff_errors=-5`, `net_bandit_issues=0` yields `total_net=-2` and therefore `SAFE`, despite the fix having added three type errors.
FOLLOW: This directly affects immune Stage 4 because SAFE/NEUTRAL results mark findings verified. A fix that regresses correctness or security in one dimension can still be accepted if style/type/security improvements elsewhere overcompensate numerically. That creates silently wrong verification, which is HIGH under the PoC standard, and can prematurely close bugs through the verified-fix path in later rounds. It also makes the tool counts non-monotonic in a misleading way: “no new issues introduced” is promised in the docstring but not actually enforced.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — declare `HARMFUL` if any individual net field is positive (`net_type_errors > 0 or net_ruff_errors > 0 or net_bandit_issues > 0`); only declare `SAFE` when at least one field is negative and none are positive. Keep the existing test-failure rule unchanged.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F003
SEVERITY: 0.74
FLAW_CLASS: 2
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.42
DESCRIPTION: FIND — `_find_target_file()` can select the wrong file by substring containment instead of an exact/relative-path match. Evidence: it extracts `*.py` substrings from finding text, then returns the first `source_path` where `sp_path.endswith(match) or match in sp_path`. The `match in sp_path` branch is unsafe: a mention like `brain.py` matches `/repo/bench/insect_brain.py`; `endocrine.py` could match a backup path containing that token; short names collide across modules.
FOLLOW: Wrong target-file selection makes fix evaluation operate on unrelated code. Baseline counts are taken from one file, the patch is applied to another, and the verdict is still attributed to `finding.finding_id`. Downstream, the immune pipeline may mark a fix verified for the wrong bug, and the sandbox signal becomes deceptive rather than merely noisy. Because endocrine is used as infrastructure between rounds, this kind of mis-targeting can silently poison multiple rounds of verification.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — remove the broad `match in sp_path` heuristic and match only on normalized exact basename equality or full relative-path suffix equality (`endswith(os.sep + match)` or exact basename match when unique). If no unique match exists, return `None` so the evaluation becomes `UNEVALUABLE` instead of patching the wrong file.
VERIFIED: TRUE

FINDING_ID: F004
SEVERITY: 0.68
FLAW_CLASS: 5
ABSTRACTION_INDEX: 0.39
DESCRIPTION: FIND — `run_mypy()` can silently return zero diagnostics on normal mypy failure modes because it parses only stdout with a narrow regex and ignores stderr/exit-status-driven fatal messages. Evidence: after `_run_tool(cmd)`, the function checks only `result.stderr == "NOT_FOUND"` and then iterates `for line in result.stdout.splitlines()`. Any invocation/config error or fatal message emitted on stderr yields `[]`, which is indistinguishable from “no mypy issues”.
FOLLOW: In `scan_health()`, this undercounts type diagnostics and makes the health monitor claim a healthier codebase than observed. In `evaluate_fix()`, pre/post mypy is not used, but the main advertised health scan is affected: reviewers and pacing logic consuming `HealthScan` can miss genuine typing failures if mypy reports via stderr. This is especially problematic because the module claims mechanical extraction from tool execution, but here stderr-based failures collapse to clean health.
PROPOSED_FIX: FIX — in `run_mypy()`, if stdout produced no parsed diagnostics and stderr is non-empty (other than `NOT_FOUND`/`TIMEOUT` handling already tracked elsewhere), emit one `ToolDiagnostic` representing a mypy execution/parsing failure with category `UNKNOWN` and severity `error`, using stderr text as the message.
VERIFIED: FALSE
